claims.text: The selected high-entropy alloy has uncharacterized superconducting behavior.
Formation of a stable crystal structure governs whether superconductivity emerges at low temperature.
Robustness of the electronic structure against lattice compression governs whether superconductivity emerges.
Scanning tunneling microscopy or spectroscopy can tune the stable crystal structure or the electronic structure's robustness against compression.
Using scanning tunneling microscopy or spectroscopy will cause superconductivity to emerge relative to a nonsuperconducting baseline.
The starting-state baseline has no superconductivity.
The hypothesis is limited to the low-temperature regime.
The relationship between crystal-structure stability and electronic-structure robustness is not well understood.
The superconducting critical temperature can be measured using scanning tunneling microscopy or spectroscopy before and after pressure is applied.
If the superconducting critical temperature does not change under pressure, the proposed mechanism is falsified.

contradictions.description: An uncharacterized superconducting state does not establish the definite baseline claim of no superconductivity.

Robustness against lattice compression would ordinarily be compatible with little or no pressure-induced change in superconducting behavior, yet the proposed rule treats an unchanged critical temperature as falsifying that robustness.
The named intervention is a characterization method, whereas the experiment's actual physical perturbation is pressure; the hypothesis incorrectly presents measurement as the tuning intervention.
